title: Large-Scale Data Processing
description: Understand MapReduce, Spark RDDs, Flink event-time processing, batch versus stream paradigms, and Lambda/Kappa architectures.

segments.text: When your data grows to petabytes, a single machine cannot process it. You need frameworks that distribute computation across thousands of nodes. Let's explore the evolution of large-scale data processing.

MapReduce, Google's pioneering framework. Two phases: Map transforms each input record into key-value pairs. Reduce aggregates all values sharing the same key. Simple, powerful, and embarrassingly parallel.

But MapReduce has a flaw. Every job reads from disk and writes back to disk. Chain three MapReduce jobs together, and you have six disk round-trips. For iterative algorithms like PageRank, this is painfully slow.

Enter Apache Spark. It keeps intermediate data in memory using Resilient Distributed Datasets, or RDDs. An RDD is an immutable, partitioned collection that tracks its lineage for fault recovery. Ten to a hundred times faster than MapReduce.
Here is a critical distinction to understand.
segments.thought_prompt: What is the difference between batch processing and stream processing? When would you choose each?

segments.text: Batch processes bounded datasets, all data is available upfront. Stream processes unbounded data as it arrives. Batch optimizes throughput, stream optimizes latency. Most real systems need both.

Apache Flink treats everything as a stream. Batch is just a bounded stream. Flink's killer feature is event-time processing. It handles out-of-order events using watermarks, tracking how far the event timeline has progressed.

The Lambda architecture runs batch and stream in parallel. The batch layer provides accurate but slow results. The speed layer provides fast but approximate results. A serving layer merges both views. The downside? You maintain two separate codebases.

The Kappa architecture simplifies things. Use only stream processing for everything. Reprocess historical data by replaying the event log. One codebase, one pipeline. Flink and Kafka together make this practical.

MapReduce for simple batch ETL. Spark for iterative analytics and machine learning. Flink for real-time event processing. Choose based on latency requirements, data characteristics, and team expertise.

segments.thought_prompt: You need real-time fraud detection AND daily financial reports. Would you use Lambda or Kappa architecture? Why?

segments.text: The answer depends on your team's capacity to maintain dual pipelines. Lambda gives accuracy guarantees from the batch layer. Kappa gives operational simplicity. In practice, many companies start with Lambda and migrate toward Kappa as their streaming infrastructure matures.
